clue.text: Finale of "Exultet" during which I leave pasta out of sight

indicators.note: the pasta piece sits in the middle of that closing stretch, during it
the closing stretch of the word Exultet is taken, everything after its opening pair
the letter I is told to leave the pasta, so it is dropped

parts.note: ravioli is a stuffed pasta
taken as written

explanation.surface: During the last bars of the Easter hymn Exultet, the singer slips some pasta out of view.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exultet is the Easter Vigil hymn; its finale ULTET has RAVIOL (RAVIOLI with I leaving) inserted.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultraviolet light lies beyond the violet end of the spectrum, so it cannot be seen by the eye.

clue.text: On time, Roy's team appear in old letter on which all agree …

indicators.note: the pieces turn up inside the old letter, appearing within it

parts.note: uncial is an old rounded style of manuscript letter
taken as written
Roy of the Rovers is a British football comic strip; his team is Melchester Rovers

explanation.surface: Football fans agree their club is in an old script, with the ellipsis leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy of the Rovers is a long-running British football comic strip, and an uncial is a rounded capital script of early manuscripts.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nobody disputes is a matter on which all agree, an exact paraphrase of the adjective.

clue.text: … are necessary to make effect of sun disappear

parts.note: a tan is what sunshine does to the skin
to go is to vanish or disappear

explanation.surface: Something is needed to make a suntan fade away, following on from the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue numbers run on: 1-down's 'on which all agree' leads to '2 … are necessary to make', the saying 'it takes two to tango'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says it takes two to do this dance, so two people are necessary to make one.

clue.text: Venetian soldier takes on 10

parts.note: a soldier ant is a caste of ant, so soldier gives ant
taken as written
the number 10 written as the letters I and O, one and zero

explanation.surface: A soldier from Venice takes on the number ten.
explanation.walkthrough: The 10 is read as its digits, a one and a zero, which look like the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is the merchant of Venice in Shakespeare's play, a Venetian character by name.

clue.text: Setter's number said to be wrong

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself says I'm, I am
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
something said is spoken, or oral

explanation.surface: A crossword setter's phone number is claimed to be incorrect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' looks like a sound signal but simply means ORAL; 'Setter's' is the setter's I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Immoral behaviour is ethically wrong, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Look attractive to painter with woodbine

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
nice means pleasant or attractive
RA stands for Royal Academician, a painter

explanation.surface: Someone looks pretty to an artist when holding honeysuckle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lonicera is the botanical genus of honeysuckle, the plant also called woodbine in Britain.

clue.text: Like "American" or "adventurer", taking cabs literally at random

indicators.note: the letters come out at random, in no set order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Words like American and adventurer are made by grabbing taxis and letters at random.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' looks part of the phrase 'at random' but it is fodder: CABS LITERALLY AT scrambled. 'taking' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both example words have four syllables, which is what this adjective describes.

clue.text: Don't talk of university when restricted by immobiliser

indicators.note: the university letter is held in by the immobiliser, restricted inside it

parts.note: a wheel clamp immobilises a car

explanation.surface: Keep quiet about the university when its car is clamped.
explanation.definitionFit: To clam up is an idiom for falling silent and refusing to talk.

clue.text: Interrupt reference to Inferno by the French

parts.note: heck is a mild euphemism for hell, the Inferno
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Someone breaks into a discussion of Dante's Inferno in French.
explanation.definitionFit: To heckle is to interrupt a speaker with shouted remarks.

clue.text: Securing device to pass back to Danish king

indicators.note: the mountain pass is to be read back to front

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
Knut (Canute) was a Danish king of England

explanation.surface: A fastener for passing on to a Danish monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A locknut is a second nut screwed down to secure the first, a fixing device.

clue.text: Slow swimmer to take up position at opening of a hole

parts.note: to man a post is to take up position at it
on a golf course a hole opens at a tee, where play starts

explanation.surface: A sluggish swimmer settles at the start of a golf hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hole' is a golf hole, which begins at a tee, so the phrase supplies the article as well.
explanation.definitionFit: The manatee or sea cow is a large, slow-moving marine mammal.

clue.text: Women in bother with Queen (as she became on January 1 1947?)

indicators.note: the words are put in a state of bother, upset into a new order

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Women in a fuss alongside the Queen, with a historical aside.
explanation.walkthrough: On 1 January 1947 Britain's coal mines were nationalised, so the Crown, the state 'she', took over the pits.
explanation.definitionFit: Nationalisation put the coal mines in state hands, so the Crown became their proprietor.

clue.text: Snooker accessory opposite to 20?

definitions.meaning: players rub this on the cue tip in snooker
the saying 'as different as ... and cheese', with 20-down

explanation.surface: Something used at the snooker table, and the opposite of another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As different as chalk and cheese' is a British idiom for complete opposites.
explanation.definitionFit: Snooker players chalk their cues, and chalk is proverbially the opposite of cheese.

clue.text: A lot of reading opposite to 23?

indicators.note: only a large part of the word is kept, losing its tail

parts.note: perusal means a reading, a careful read-through

explanation.surface: Plenty of reading, set against another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From China to Peru' is an old phrase meaning from one end of the world to the other, so Peru opposes 23-down.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'from China to Peru' places the two countries at opposite ends of the earth.

clue.text: High quality fellow with fellow — sorry, cello — player

indicators.note: a player of the cello works on its letters, rearranging them

explanation.surface: A top-class man and his partner, apologising to a cellist.
explanation.walkthrough: The car firm is named after two fellows, Charles Rolls and Henry Royce, and the name also means top quality.
explanation.definitionFit: The marque is a byword for top quality and names a partnership of two men.

clue.text: Unusual day follows below opposite to 1 across

indicators.note: the unusual day comes after, following the word for below

parts.note: inf. is the abbreviation for infra, Latin for below, used in footnotes
rare means unusual

explanation.surface: An odd day comes after something beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inf.' (infra) means 'below' in references, as in 'vide infra'.
explanation.definitionFit: Infrared lies beyond the red end of the spectrum, at the opposite end from ultraviolet.

clue.text: Vicar's stipend above subsistence level?

parts.note: a living is a vicar's church post, or benefice
a stipend is a wage or salary

explanation.surface: A clergyman's pay, perhaps better than bare survival.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'living' is the old name for a parish post held by a vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: A living wage is pay sufficient for a decent life, more than bare subsistence.

clue.text: Copper in "Missing Persons" finds destroyer

indicators.note: the copper goes inside the missing persons

parts.note: people who are missing are lost
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A policeman in the missing persons unit tracks down a wrecker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer but is the metal, symbol CU.
explanation.definitionFit: Locust swarms destroy crops, so the insect is a destroyer.

clue.text: Instrument used while street is enclosed

indicators.note: the street is shut inside the word for while

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tool is used as a road is fenced off.
explanation.definitionFit: A whistle is a simple wind instrument, like the tin whistle.

clue.text: Weighty matter for whale?

parts.note: a gram is a unit of weight
pus is matter from a wound

explanation.surface: A heavy question about a whale.
explanation.definitionFit: Grampus is the name for Risso's dolphin and, loosely, the killer whale, a cetacean.

clue.text: King abandoning obstacle to political grouping

indicators.note: the king leaves, so his letter is taken away

parts.note: a block is an obstacle
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch leaves a hurdle for a party alliance.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is an alliance of countries or parties acting together.

clue.text: Big fellow, it sometimes has to be said

definitions.text: it sometimes has to be said
definitions.meaning: photographers ask people to say ... to make them smile

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big fellow' is cut from the idiom 'big cheese', a VIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese gives the idiom for a bigwig and the word said for photographs.

clue.text: One who is responsible for progress in profession lacking energy

indicators.note: the energy letter is missing, so it is taken out

parts.note: a career is one's progress through a profession
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone in charge of a career that has run out of steam.
explanation.definitionFit: A carer looks after a dependant, so is the person responsible for them.

clue.text: Blair is Church of England — about to cross

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, a Church of England man, is about to get angry.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair was an Anglican who became a Catholic; 'to' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Irascible means quick to anger, easily made cross.

clue.text: Mate for tea?

definitions.meaning: the best cups and saucers for tea are fine porcelain

explanation.walkthrough: 'China plate' is Cockney rhyming slang for 'mate', shortened to its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: China is Cockney slang for a friend and the porcelain teaset.

clue.text: Re-entering, circumvent water plant

indicators.note: the short word goes into the other

parts.note: to skirt something is to go round it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Coming back in, a plant in the water is bypassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Re-entering' looks like one word but splits into RE plus the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Skirret is a waterside plant of the parsley family grown for its roots.

clue.text: Royals entail costs when given new heart

indicators.note: the costs are given a new piece added to them
the added piece goes into the middle, the heart

parts.note: prices are costs

explanation.surface: Members of the royal family incur expenses after a heart transplant.
explanation.definitionFit: Princes are male members of a royal family.

clue.text: Somewhat ludicrous American composer lacking success completely somewhere in Wiltshire

indicators.note: only some of the word is used, its opening
the success part is taken away from the composer

parts.note: George Gershwin was an American composer
a win is a success
all means completely

explanation.surface: A rather silly American composer fails completely somewhere in Wiltshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Ludgershall is a small town in Wiltshire, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludgershall is a town in Wiltshire, so the place name fits the vague location.
